covers.quote: Use them only if people recognise and understand them.

rules.quote: Choose acronyms and initialisms people will recognise
rules.specification: Recognition depends on the intended users and the explanations available to them. The page supplies no fixed familiarity threshold.
rules.violation_condition: An acronym or initialism is used that the intended users are unlikely to recognise or understand in context, even with the explanation provided.
when: Assess understanding in context; an unfamiliar shortened form can be made understandable by an explanation.
rules.why: G-4: the heading and introductory instruction express one audience-understanding check.

covers.quote: Define them the first time you use them in content (unless you’re certain all users will understand them without a definition – consult a dictionary first).
If there’s a chance users won’t know the meaning of an acronym or initialism, define it at first mention.
Write the term in full first and follow with the acronym or initialism in parentheses.
Write well-known acronyms or initialisms first and follow with the full term in parentheses.
You don’t need to define some acronyms and initialisms on first use.
some place names (NT, ACT)
time of day (am, pm)
some organisational names (BHP, Qantas)
terms that began as acronyms but are now words in their own right (radar, scuba, sonar).

examples.note: The familiar shortened form precedes its expansion.

parts.quote: All living organisms have DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) within their cells. DNA tells cells what proteins to make.

rules.quote: Spell out most acronyms on first use
rules.specification: Whether users need a definition depends on audience knowledge. Treat the introduction and its order as one check: normally full term (shortened form), but shortened form (full term) for well-known forms that are explained.
rules.violation_condition: A shortened form needing explanation lacks a definition at first mention, or its introduction lacks the required full-term/shortened-form pairing and parentheses in the appropriate order.
when: Applies to acronyms and initialisms at their first mention.
Define the shortened form if there is a chance users will not know its meaning.
A definition is unnecessary if all users will understand the shortened form without one.
For well-known forms that are explained, put the shortened form first and the full term in parentheses.
Examples not needing a first-use definition include NT, ACT, am, pm, BHP and Qantas.
Words in their own right, such as radar, scuba and sonar, do not need first-use definitions.
rules.why: G-2–G-4: first-use definition, ordering cases and exemptions belong to one introduction check; later mentions are separate.

rules.quote: Include them with their spelt-out forms in the glossary.
rules.violation_condition: A shortened form used in the content is missing from an accompanying glossary, or its glossary entry lacks its spelt-out form.
when: Applies where the content has a glossary.
Particularly important for content containing many specialist shortened forms.
rules.why: G-1: glossary completeness is a specific child check, distinct from whether a glossary must be provided.

covers.quote: Repeat the full term if the user needs it
If you use the shortened form only a few times in long-form content, consider writing out the full term more than once.
People could come across the shortened form without reading the text where it is first defined.
For example, a user might click straight to a section that only includes the shortened form.

examples.note: The second mention uses the established shortened form.

parts.quote: The Department of Social Services (DSS) manages a range of benefits and payments for eligible Australians. DSS helps support communities through a number of programs and services.

rules.quote: Use the shortened form rather than the full term for later mentions.
rules.specification: The page does not quantify ‘a few times’ or ‘long-form’, or define exactly when users need a reminder. Sparse use is a reason to consider repetition, not an automatic requirement to repeat at every occurrence.
rules.violation_condition: A later mention unnecessarily repeats the full term instead of the established shortened form, or uses only the shortened form where users need the full term repeated.
when: Applies after the shortened form has been introduced.
Normally prefer the shortened form for later mentions.
Repeat the full term where users need it, particularly when a shortened form appears only a few times in long-form content.
Consider users who enter a section without reading the first definition.
rules.why: G-2–G-3: later-mention choices and reader-needed repetitions are conditional cases of one check.

covers.quote: Rather than using acronyms or initialisms, it can be easier for people if you:
spell out the agency’s name in full the first time you use it
This is usually more useful to non-specialist users.

examples.note: A full name is followed by a generic reference.

parts.quote: The Bureau of Meteorology prepares Australia’s official weather forecasts. The bureau provides its forecasts on its website.

examples.note: A full name is followed by a generic reference.

parts.quote: The Department of Finance is in Canberra. The department supports government financial management.

rules.quote: then use the generic name (‘department’, ‘agency’, ‘bureau’) afterwards.
rules.specification: This is a readability preference, not a ban on government acronyms. Apply where a generic reference is unambiguous and easier for the intended non-specialist users.
rules.violation_condition: Later references to a government organisation use an acronym or initialism where a generic name would be clearer and more useful to non-specialist users.
when: Introduce the organisation by its full name first.
The preference is particularly relevant to non-specialist users.
rules.why: G-2: the full-name introduction and subsequent generic references form one preferred naming sequence.

covers.quote: For content with many specialised acronyms and initialisms, provide a glossary – a list of terms and their meaning that users can refer to.
You don’t need to include a glossary if:
there are only a few unfamiliar shortened forms
each one is only in a very limited section of text
each one is spelt out when first mentioned.

rules.quote: Include a list if content relies on many acronyms and initialisms
rules.specification: The page gives no numerical thresholds for ‘many’, ‘a few’ or ‘a very limited section’. Read the three exemption conditions together; no numerical cut-off is assumed.
rules.violation_condition: Content containing many specialised acronyms or initialisms has no glossary of their meanings and does not meet the stated exemption.
when: Applies to content with many specialised acronyms and initialisms.
A glossary is unnecessary when there are only a few unfamiliar shortened forms, each is confined to a very limited section, and each is spelt out at first mention.
rules.why: G-2–G-4: the heading, body instruction and exemption describe one glossary-presence check.

covers.quote: The glossary usually appears before the references (with the endmatter).

rules.quote: Include the glossary at the end of the content or on a separate webpage.
rules.violation_condition: A glossary is placed somewhere other than the end of the content or a separate webpage.
when: Applies where a glossary is provided.
For print, placement before the references with the endmatter counts as placement at the end.
rules.why: G-2: print placement qualifies one location check; location is distinct from glossary presence.

rules.quote: Use a hyperlink in the text to help people access the glossary.
rules.violation_condition: Electronic content with a glossary has no in-text hyperlink that gives access to it.
when: Applies where a glossary is provided and the content supports hyperlinks.
Does not apply to print-only copies.
rules.why: G-1: access by hyperlink is a separate check from glossary provision and placement.

covers.quote: Don’t place a full stop after the acronym or initialism.
The exception is if the shortened form ends a sentence and isn’t followed by another punctuation mark.

parts.quote: Will you be attending COAG this month?
I’m working on a B2B project at the moment.
She’s now working in FOI.
Is the company being investigated by ASIC?

rules.quote: Don’t end acronyms and initialisms with a full stop
rules.violation_condition: A full stop follows an acronym or initialism where it is not needed to end the sentence, including where another punctuation mark ends the sentence.
when: A sentence-ending full stop is allowed after the shortened form when no other punctuation mark ends the sentence.
rules.why: G-2–G-4: the body restates the heading, and sentence-ending punctuation is an exception to the same check.

covers.quote: Acronyms are usually all capitals, but use lower case for some familiar acronyms (taser, captcha, laser).
Use an initial capital for familiar acronyms that are proper nouns (Qantas, Anzac).
Initialisms are often all upper case (VOIP, FOI) but there are exceptions (bpm).

rules.quote: Use capitals for most acronyms and initialisms
rules.violation_condition: An acronym or initialism has capitalisation inconsistent with its established form: normally all capitals, but lower case or an initial capital where the established exception requires it.
when: Most acronyms and initialisms use all capitals.
Use established lower-case forms for familiar acronyms such as taser, captcha and laser.
Familiar proper-noun acronyms such as Qantas and Anzac take an initial capital.
Initialisms can have established lower-case exceptions, such as bpm.
rules.why: G-2: upper-case, lower-case and initial-capital forms are cases of one shortened-form capitalisation check.

covers.quote: If the acronym or initialism represents a proper noun, start each word with a capital letter (excluding words such as ‘of’ and ‘and’).

parts.quote: EIS for ‘environmental impact statement’
TB for ‘tuberculosis’
ASIO [Australian Security Intelligence Organisation]
OPC [Office of Parliamentary Counsel]
NSW [New South Wales]
ILSC [Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation]

rules.quote: If the acronym or initialism represents common nouns, don’t begin each word of the full form with a capital letter.
rules.violation_condition: An expanded full form is capitalised as a proper name when it consists of common nouns, or lacks the required word-initial capitals when it is a proper name.
when: Common-noun full forms do not inherit capital letters from their acronyms or initialisms.
For proper-noun full forms, capitalise each word except connecting words such as ‘of’ and ‘and’.
Ordinary sentence-initial capitalisation is not an error under the common-noun case.
rules.why: G-2: common-noun and proper-noun expansions are conditional cases of one full-form capitalisation check.

covers.quote: Avoid using the plural or possessive of an acronym or initialism when you define it.

parts.quote: It’s compulsory for certain businesses to have an Australian Business Number (ABN). The Australian Business Register manages applications for ABNs.
The University of New South Wales (UNSW) has a new student policy. UNSW’s policy is popular with its staff and students.

rules.quote: Avoid plural and possessive forms on the first use
rules.violation_condition: An acronym or initialism is introduced in its defining construction in a plural or possessive form.
when: Applies when the shortened form is defined.
Plural and possessive forms in later mentions are outside this restriction.
rules.why: G-2–G-4: plural and possessive introductions are cases of one defining-form restriction, restated in the body.

covers.quote: Quote acronyms and initialisms the same way as the speaker
When quoting an exact phrase, write exactly what the speaker said.

rules.quote: If they used an acronym or initialism, quote it.
rules.specification: Verifying fidelity requires access to the source quotation or recording; it cannot be established from the finished quotation alone.
rules.violation_condition: A direct quotation replaces or otherwise changes an acronym or initialism that the speaker actually used.
when: Applies when quoting an exact phrase.
An explanatory full term may be added in square brackets without replacing the speaker’s shortened form.
rules.why: G-4: the heading and exact-quotation instruction support one check on preserving the speaker’s shortened form.

parts.quote: ‘We’re continuing to manage the number of SES [Senior Executive Service] to ensure the Public Service isn’t top heavy,’ he said.

rules.specification: Audience recognition requires contextual judgement. Preserve the source’s ‘or’: either possible unfamiliarity or the absence of an earlier explanation triggers the bracketed expansion.

Add the full term in square brackets if users might not recognise it.

anchor.quote: Use a hyperlink in the text to help people access the glossary.

tags.violation_condition: Electronic content with a glossary has no in-text hyperlink that gives access to it.

when: Applies where a glossary is provided and the content supports hyperlinks.
Does not apply to print-only copies.
rules.why: G-1: access by hyperlink is a separate check from glossary provision and placement.

anchor.quote: Don’t end acronyms and initialisms with a full stop

covers.quote: Don’t place a full stop after the acronym or initialism.
The exception is if the shortened form ends a sentence and isn’t followed by another punctuation mark.

parts.quote: Will you be attending COAG this month?
I’m working on a B2B project at the moment.
She’s now working in FOI.
Is the company being investigated by ASIC?

tags.violation_condition: A full stop follows an acronym or initialism where it is not needed to end the sentence, including where another punctuation mark ends the sentence.

when: A sentence-ending full stop is allowed after the shortened form when no other punctuation mark ends the sentence.
rules.why: G-2–G-4: the body restates the heading, and sentence-ending punctuation is an exception to the same check.

anchor.quote: Use capitals for most acronyms and initialisms

covers.quote: Acronyms are usually all capitals, but use lower case for some familiar acronyms (taser, captcha, laser).
covers.suffix: Use an initial capital for fami

covers.quote: Use an initial capital for familiar acronyms that are proper nouns (Qantas, Anzac).
Initialisms are often all upper case (VOIP, FOI) but there are exceptions (bpm).

tags.violation_condition: An acronym or initialism has capitalisation inconsistent with its established form: normally all capitals, but lower case or an initial capital where the established exception requires it.

when: Most acronyms and initialisms use all capitals.
Use established lower-case forms for familiar acronyms such as taser, captcha and laser.
Familiar proper-noun acronyms such as Qantas and Anzac take an initial capital.
Initialisms can have established lower-case exceptions, such as bpm.
rules.why: G-2: upper-case, lower-case and initial-capital forms are cases of one shortened-form capitalisation check.

anchor.quote: If the acronym or initialism represents common nouns, don’t begin each word of the full form with a capital letter.

covers.quote: If the acronym or initialism represents a proper noun, start each word with a capital letter (excluding words such as ‘of’ and ‘and’).

parts.quote: EIS for ‘environmental impact statement’
TB for ‘tuberculosis’
ASIO [Australian Security Intelligence Organisation]
OPC [Office of Parliamentary Counsel]
NSW [New South Wales]
ILSC [Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation]

tags.violation_condition: An expanded full form is capitalised as a proper name when it consists of common nouns, or lacks the required word-initial capitals when it is a proper name.

when: Common-noun full forms do not inherit capital letters from their acronyms or initialisms.
For proper-noun full forms, capitalise each word except connecting words such as ‘of’ and ‘and’.
Ordinary sentence-initial capitalisation is not an error under the common-noun case.
rules.why: G-2: common-noun and proper-noun expansions are conditional cases of one full-form capitalisation check.

anchor.quote: Avoid plural and possessive forms on the first use

covers.quote: Avoid using the plural or possessive of an acronym or initialism when you define it.
covers.suffix: This makes it easy for users to

parts.quote: It’s compulsory for certain businesses to have an Australian Business Number (ABN). The Australian Business Register manages applications for ABNs.
parts.suffix: [There’s no need to use an apos

parts.quote: The University of New South Wales (UNSW) has a new student policy. UNSW’s policy is popular with its staff and students.

tags.violation_condition: An acronym or initialism is introduced in its defining construction in a plural or possessive form.

when: Applies when the shortened form is defined.
Plural and possessive forms in later mentions are outside this restriction.
rules.why: G-2–G-4: plural and possessive introductions are cases of one defining-form restriction, restated in the body.

anchor.quote: If they used an acronym or initialism, quote it.
anchor.suffix: Show the full term in square br

covers.quote: Quote acronyms and initialisms the same way as the speaker
When quoting an exact phrase, write exactly what the speaker said.
covers.suffix: If they used an acronym or init

tags.specification: Verifying fidelity requires access to the source quotation or recording; it cannot be established from the finished quotation alone.
tags.violation_condition: A direct quotation replaces or otherwise changes an acronym or initialism that the speaker actually used.

when: Applies when quoting an exact phrase.
An explanatory full term may be added in square brackets without replacing the speaker’s shortened form.
rules.why: G-4: the heading and exact-quotation instruction support one check on preserving the speaker’s shortened form.

anchor.quote: Show the full term in square brackets if users might not recognise the term or if you haven’t already explained it.

parts.quote: ‘We’re continuing to manage the number of SES [Senior Executive Service] to ensure the Public Service isn’t top heavy,’ he said.

tags.specification: Audience recognition requires contextual judgement. Preserve the source’s ‘or’: either possible unfamiliarity or the absence of an earlier explanation triggers the bracketed expansion.
tags.violation_condition: An acronym or initialism in a direct quotation lacks its full term in square brackets when users might not recognise it or it has not already been explained.

when: Applies to acronyms and initialisms in exact quotations.
Add the full term in square brackets if users might not recognise it.
Also add it if the term has not already been explained.
rules.why: G-2: the two alternative triggers govern one bracketed-expansion check, separate from quotation fidelity.
